newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - BRITISH BUSINESS PRESS - DEC 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - BRITISH BUSINESS PRESS - DEC 5.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company.
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- WILLIAMS TO SELL OFF 15 COMPANIES IN BRITAIN

Williams Holdings has agreed to sell 15 of its British heating, construction and home products businesses, including Valor gas fires, Rawlplug and Smallbone kitchens to management for 360 million stg. Seventy managers will be investing over one million stg of equity in the buyout, and will be rewarded if the business goes well and is floated. William is to retain a 26 percent stake in the buyout vehicle, which may be floated in two to four years' time.
-- GRANADA SELLS FLAGSHIP HOTEL TO SAUDI PRINCE

Granada have agreed to sell the George V hotel in Paris to Prince al Waleed bin Talal for 104 million stg. His last minute offer succeeded in winning the luxury hotel from the Sultan of Brunei. Granada had agreed on a three-week exclusive negotiation period with the sultan which ended without an offer being made. The George V is the most prestigious in Granada's Exclusive portfolio, which was acquired as part of the 3.9 billion stg takeover of Forte FTE.L at the beginning of the year.
-- BASHAM 'REGISTED CALLS' OVER STORIES ON VIRGIN

A High Court jury has heard that Brian Basham, British Airways' outside PR man in its battle against Richard Branson's Virgin Atlantic, specialised in using sleaze as widely and discreetly as possible to discredit serious businessmen and help them "fall over the edge". Mr Basham denied he ever passed on "distasteful, discreditable or irrelevant" facts about Mr Branson, and said he resisted the demands of BA's chairman, Lord King, and chief executive, Sir Colin Marshall, to spread unsubstantiated stories on Virgin.
THE TIMES
-- BASS TOASTS 7,000 NEW JOBS

The brewing and leisure company Bass plans to create 7,000 jobs in its pubs and leisure businesses with a 670 million stg expansion plan. Chairman Sir Ian Prosser said the jobs would be concentrated in its branded pubs and businesses, including All Bar One, Fork and Pitcher and Harvester, and 1,500 jobs will be created through the expansion of its bowling parks and the adult orientated electronic theme parks, Dave and Busters. Bass also unveiled a 12 percent profit before tax.
-- DELTA IN TALKS TO CREATE WORLD'S LARGEST CARRIER

The world's largest carrier could be created with the possible merger of Delta Airlines, the third-largest American carrier, and Continental Airlines. This could trigger a wave of consolidation in the US airline industry. A takeover of Continental, the fifth-largest, could be worth 1.8 billion dollars. The combined company would have about one quarter of America's domestic market and would serve about 155 cities inside the US.
-- BOARD PAY STILL RISING FASTER THAN WORKERS'

The latest top wages study from the Institute of Directors and Reward, the pay research group, shows that boardroom pay is rising faster than in previous years, with average increases for company directors reaching five percent. On average over the past 12 months directors received rises of between 3.7 percent and five percent, ahead of rank-and-file company employees. Directors forecast further increases in the coming year.
THE GUARDIAN
-- UNCARING BANKS UNDER FIRE

In his annual report, Laurence Shurman, the Banking Ombudsman, has attacked banks for taking too little care when closing branches and cutting jobs, saying it had led to some "horrendous cases of maladministration". He disclosed there had been a 22 percent increase in telephone complaints and inquiries. Mr Shurman said that some of the worst cases appeared to stem from banks' attempts to achieve greater efficiency.
-- CONTROLS TO BE TIGHTENED ON LONDON'S ALTERNATIVE MARKET

The Stock Exchange has unveiled plans to tighten the screws on the Alternative Investment Market, on which shares in nearly 250 companies are being traded. The plans include demands that they issue a "wealth warning" to would-be investors. The move comes amid growing criticism of inadequate controls on companies listed on the secondary market, the capitalisation of which has soared to more than five billion stg since its launch last year.
-- CARLTON LOOKS AT PAY-TV FOR PROFIT

Carlton Communications media group has said it is planning to expand it pay-TV interests with moves into cable, satellite and digital broadcasting. The group hinted that more takeovers could follow its purchase of Westcountry TV to make Carlton the first ITV company to control three licenses. In order to renegotiate the annual amount Carlton pays to the government in return for its broadcast licence, the group will separate out the broadcast regions it controls -- Carlton, Central and Westcountry.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- LEGAL THREAT TO DOMESTIC POWER FREE-FOR-ALL

The electricity industry regulator, Stephen Littlechild, has been warned by lawyers acting for the 12 regional electricity companies and the two Scottish power producers that his plans to open up the domestic market to full competition in 1998 are unlawful. The lawyers claim that the proposed regulatory framework would prevent electricity suppliers from recovering unpaid bills or disconnecting customers outside their own franchise areas who refuse to pay.
-- 10,000 JOBS TO GO IN NATWEST BRANCHES

NatWest have announced plans to cut at least 10,000 jobs in its high street banking operations in the next four to five years, leaving 27,000 high street staff by 2001. The cuts are the result of the group's plans to build a "new retail bank", and have confirmed the fears of the banking union, Bifu, which warned of the job losses earlier in the year. NatWest aims to have 1,750 branches by the year 2001, which means the closure of 300 branches.
-- FRENCH GOVERNMENT SUSPENDS THOMSON SALE

The French government has suspended the sale of Thomson, the defence and electronics giant, to a consortium which includes British Aerospace. The move was prompted by a wave of public protests against the proposed selling of Thomson Multimedia to the South Korean conglomerate Daewoo. The French Finance Ministry said its Privatisation Commission had declared itself incapable of giving a favorable opinion to Lagardere, which was chosen as the preferred bidder for Thomson in October, because of the terms of Daewoo's purchase of Thomson Multimedia.
